clinicalPearls: Classic triad of congenital ichthyosis, spastic diplegia or tetraplegia, and intellectual disability
The ichthyosis is generalised with fine to plate-like scaling, often prominent in flexures, and pruritus is characteristic
A pathognomonic ophthalmological sign is glistening white/yellow dots (crystalline maculopathy) at the macula
Autosomal recessive; caused by mutations in ALDH3A2 encoding fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase (FALDH)
Neurological features typically emerge in infancy with delayed motor milestones and spasticity, and seizures may occur
Photophobia and reduced visual acuity accompany the macular changes
Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics for the skin, physiotherapy and spasticity care, and specialist neurological and ophthalmological follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Sjogren-Larsson syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in ALDH3A2, which encodes fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase, a component of the fatty alcohol:NAD oxidoreductase complex. Deficient enzyme activity blocks the oxidation of long-chain fatty aldehydes and alcohols, which accumulate and are incorporated abnormally into lipids. In the epidermis this disrupts the lamellar lipid membranes essential for the permeability barrier, producing ichthyosis; in the developing central nervous system abnormal lipid metabolism and myelin disturbance underlie the spasticity and cognitive impairment; and lipid deposition in the retina produces the characteristic glistening macular dots.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital ichthyoses (lamellar ichthyosis, congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma)
Refsum disease and other peroxisomal disorders
Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome (neutral lipid storage disease with ichthyosis)
Cerebral palsy of other cause with coincidental xerosis
additionalInvestigations: Assay of fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase activity in cultured fibroblasts or leucocytes
Ophthalmological examination for glistening macular dots and photophobia
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (white-matter change) and MR spectroscopy showing an abnormal lipid peak
Skin biopsy showing hyperkeratosis with a variably reduced or thickened granular layer
redFlags: Progressive loss of motor function or new-onset seizures
Feeding difficulty or failure to thrive in the affected infant
Barrier compromise with recurrent skin infection
reference.prognosis: Neurological impairment is usually static or slowly progressive and largely irreversible; most patients have lasting spasticity and intellectual disability. The ichthyosis and pruritus can be controlled but not cured, and lifespan varies with the severity of neurological and swallowing involvement.
pitfalls: Diagnosing isolated cerebral palsy and missing the associated ichthyosis and macular dots
Attributing pruritus to eczema rather than recognising it as a characteristic feature
Failing to arrange fundoscopy, which can reveal the near-specific glistening dots
Overlooking the recessive inheritance and the value of genetic counselling for the family
management: Control the ichthyosis with regular emollients, keratolytics such as topical urea or lactic acid, and systemic retinoids for severe scaling
Target the characteristic pruritus with leukotriene-synthesis inhibitors such as zileuton alongside antihistamines and diligent skin care
Manage spasticity with physiotherapy, antispasticity agents such as baclofen and orthotic support, and treat any seizures with antiseizure medication
Provide ophthalmology surveillance for the crystalline maculopathy and photophobia, supplying tinted lenses and low-vision support
Deliver multidisciplinary developmental support with special education and speech and occupational therapy for the intellectual disability, monitoring nutrition and swallowing
Offer genetic counselling and carrier and family testing given autosomal recessive ALDH3A2 inheritance
